I think the big thing is that machines and AI are replacing human labor instead of simply augmenting it. The industrial revolution was about enhancing human productivity, but humans were still a key part of the equation. Automation is more analogous to being a horse just before the invention of the mass produced automobile. Horses had been used as a form of rapid transport for literally thousands of years. And then somehow in a period of about 50 years they were from being responsible for nearly all land travel to serving no major commercial purpose. Telling people that in 50 years horses as transportation would have been all but completely phased out would probably have been met with more than a little skepticism.

Another big change is that AI has finally enabled effective computer vision. This has been a huge holdup in the past. Without robots being able to 'see' they're limited to very basic tasks - grasp, lift 0.2 meters, rotate 45 degrees, weld for 2 seconds, rotate -45 degrees, lower 0.2 meters, release, wait 2 seconds, repeat. With computer vision we can now change this to wait until there's an unfinished hinge in front of you, pick it up, complete the weld, then put it back on the track. That same bot can now be placed and used more or less anywhere. Give it some basic mobility and you can even get it to start positioning itself.

And the above is a completely elementary example. The ability to convert the real world into something an AI can 'understand' opens up a huge door for automating and introducing AI into nearly any task. For instance, there's been a variety of experiments with introducing AIs into surgery.

And if you take it a step further there's no real need to have these 'expert systems' or systems that are specialized for any given task. Create a generic highly mobile robot, the atlas series is a starting point example, and start giving it the 'brains' to do a wide array of tasks. Suddenly the same robot that can weld joints and flip burgers is the same robot that can also perform emergency surgery or compose a symphony.

The impact has often been unclear in that, until recently, automation rarely directly substituted for people in any particular job but rather obsolesced those jobs by changing business models or the way work/production was done. Often new technology leads to business failure as younger more adaptive companies with new business models keyed to their adoption of the new technology outcompete older companies belabored by old capital and old paradigms. And so the change rarely looks like people being replaced by machines. The jobs are lost in the 'churn' of the corporate/industrial ecology.

In the late 19th and early 20th century middle-class status was typically defined by owning a home and having a set of domestic servants. People then used to imagine the development of personal robots that would take these servants roles, allowing more people to live a middle-class lifestyle. What actually happened was that those servants became obsolesced altogether by the changes technology brought to how things worked in daily life and how we defined the middle-class lifestyle. Robots didn't replace maids, butlers, and cooks. Home appliances. automobiles, telephones, supermarkets, and factory-made food obsolesced the need for those jobs. And THATs how automation generally impacts things.

Sometimes the catalysts of automation are changes in things we don't even associate with the technology. Early in the 20th century dining was on a fast-track to automation with business models like the famous Horn & Hardart Automat. The automat was based on a dining area with walls of little glass door cabinets opened with a coin operated latch. Behind the walls kitchen staff would make foods in bulk and load the cabinets with prepared dishes. People would then serve themselves, using coins to take the items they wanted. No wait-staff was needed, just busboys to collect the used dishes and clean the dining tables. It was highly convenient, particularly in the urban environment, and automats became very popular worldwide. It looked like restaurants were soon to evolve into giant vending machines.

But after WWII automats went into decline for a peculiar reason. Food prices climbed but governments resisted adoption of larger denomination coinage. So the convenience of the automat was damaged by the need for increasing amounts of coins to operate the little food cabinets. A reliable paper money reader was very long in coming. Those didn't turn up until the late '70s. And so fast food restaurants were forced to reverse their trend in automation and resort to the counter-service model common today, needing people at the front-end once again chiefly to handle paper money. This is also why vending machines went into decline or became more specialized in products --there were simply fewer products you could afford with one to a few coins and no way to automatically read paper money. In countries that had broader coinage denomination, like Japan, vending machines flourished in great diversity.

In the '70s the problem was potentially solved not by the introduction of paper money readers, which remained bulky for some time, but by debit cards, which afforded the convenience of coin-op for purchases of things at any price. Many IT companies began developing automated PoP systems to take advantage of this new form of money. But banks, being latently racist and classist, long resisted providing access to debit cards to the demographics that most consumed fast food. It wasn't until the '90s that debit card use started becoming truly ubiquitous in the US.

Recently automation in fast-food restaurants has become a political football as CEOs shoot their mouth off with threats of 'resorting' to automation. In reality, though, the ubiquity of the debit card, and more recently digital payment through smartphones, has created this pressure to return to the level of front-end automation fast food used to have but lost. It's been coming for two decades, resisted by the fact that, now, the elderly have grown to prominence in the fast food demographic but remain averse to cash alternatives. Right now an entrepreneur could start a fast food restaurant with a phone app and a digital smart-lock for another kind of automat-like cabinet. A restaurant started in San Francisco (of course...) has now demonstrated this very model. Interestingly, the entrepreneur founding this business emphatically states that he isn't replacing any jobs --because as far as his business model is concerned, those jobs no longer exist. Thus you can see how technological job destruction plays out.
